analysis.one_liner: Restricts pharmacy middlemen's pay in Medicare drug plans to flat service fees and forces disclosure of drug rebates and pricing.
analysis.headline: Introduced July 2025 with 70 cosponsors split 39 Republicans and 31 Democrats, the bill has sat untouched in three House committees with no hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targets pharmacy benefit managers, the middlemen that insurers and Medicare drug plans hire to run prescription drug benefits. Starting in 2028, these middlemen could keep only flat, fair-market service fees — no pay tied to drug prices, and no pocketing part of manufacturer rebates. Medicare drug plans would have to open their pharmacy networks to any pharmacy meeting standard terms, pharmacies could file complaints about unfair contracts, and middlemen would have to report what they charge, what they receive in rebates, and what they keep.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare Part D enrollees, who face higher drug costs and shrinking pharmacy options as independent pharmacies close; people with employer health plans, who get new rights to see what their pharmacy middleman is paid and keeps; and independent community pharmacies, which get guaranteed access to plan networks and a complaint process against unfair contract terms.

how_it_helps.text: Requires Medicare Part D plans to allow any pharmacy that meets standard contract terms to join their networks, effective plan year 2029, ending the practice of locking independent pharmacies out of preferred networks.

Requires pharmacy benefit managers working with Part D plans, starting 2028, to accept no income other than flat-dollar, fair-market 'bona fide service fees' — not fees calculated as a percentage of a drug's price or tied to rebates and discounts.
Allows PBMs to receive manufacturer rebates only if they pass them fully through to the plan sponsor, and requires PBM affiliates to disgorge any remuneration taken in violation of the rules.

Creates a complaint process for pharmacies alleging unfair contract terms, with civil monetary penalties for plan sponsors, anti-retaliation and anti-coercion protections, and a requirement that PBMs reimburse sponsors for penalties caused by PBM violations.

Requires PBMs for both Medicare Part D plans and employer group health plans to submit detailed reports covering what they pay pharmacies per claim, what they receive in rebates and fees, what they retain, and any benefit designs steering patients to PBM-owned pharmacies; participants and beneficiaries can request a summary and claim-level information.

Directs CMS to publish reports on 'essential retail pharmacies' — the sole pharmacy in a rural, suburban, urban, or underserved area — comparing their reimbursement, fees, cost-sharing, and numbers against chain-affiliated pharmacies.

analysis.who_pays: Pharmacy benefit managers and their affiliated pharmacies would lose revenue tied to drug prices and retained rebates. Plan sponsors and insurers bear new oversight and reporting compliance costs, which could show up in premiums. Taxpayers fund roughly $322 million in appropriations to run the new enforcement and reporting system.

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates about $322 million ($188 million to CMS, $113 million to CMS for PBM oversight, $20 million to the HHS Inspector General, $1 million to MedPAC) from the Treasury to administer the new requirements.

The new network-access rules and flat-fee standards only take effect in plan years 2028 and 2029, leaving current PBM practices in place for several years, and the Secretary must first run a request for information and set contract standards before enforcement starts.

Most of the information PBMs must report stays confidential: the Secretary may not publicly disclose contract prices, rebates, or anything identifying a specific PBM, plan, or drug, so the public sees only aggregate summaries rather than the underlying pricing data.

Compliance and reporting costs for plan sponsors, insurers, and PBMs could be passed through to premiums; the bill relies heavily on HHS rulemaking, and enforcement depends on the Secretary investigating complaints 'as determined appropriate,' leaving wide discretion.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core change — cutting PBM pay that is tied to drug prices and forcing rebate pass-through — aims squarely at a documented cost driver for Medicare beneficiaries and employers, and the any-willing-pharmacy rule directly addresses the wave of independent pharmacy closures that leave many communities without a drugstore. The costs are real but modest by comparison: a few hundred million in appropriations, compliance burdens on plans, and years-long phase-ins. The biggest design weakness is secrecy — the transparency the bill creates flows to regulators and plan sponsors, not to the public, which limits both consumer benefit and public accountability.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees — Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means — and no committee has scheduled a hearing, markup, or floor vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Buddy Carter of Georgia introduced the bill on July 10, 2025, joined by 11 original cosponsors from both parties, including Reps. Debbie Dingell, Greg Murphy, Deborah Ross, Raja Krishnamoorthi, and Nicole Malliotakis.
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, additionally, to the Education and Workforce and Ways and Means Committees.
The bill attracted 70 cosponsors — 39 Republicans and 31 Democrats — within months of introduction.
The action history shows no further activity after the referral: no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the status quo: pharmacy benefit managers and their parent companies keep their current fee and rebate structures because no committee has acted, while patients and independent pharmacies wait.

for.name: Rep. Earl L. 'Buddy' Carter
for.what_they_did: Introduced the PBM Reform Act and recruited a bipartisan group of 11 original cosponsors.

for.name: 70 House cosponsors
for.role: Members of the House (39 R, 31 D)
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, signaling broad bipartisan support within three months of introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Took no recorded action — no hearings, markups, or votes — after receiving the bill in July 2025.

against.name: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts/Evernorth, Optum Rx)
against.role: Three companies controlling most U.S. prescription drug claims processing
against.what_they_did: Engaged in extensive lobbying on PBM legislation during this period, opposing measures that would end price-linked compensation; the bill sits without committee action.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is genuinely bipartisan — 39 Republicans and 31 Democrats among 70 cosponsors — with no party-line division visible in the record so far; the obstacle is committee inaction, not a partisan vote.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers (CVS Caremark, Express Scripts/Evernorth, Optum Rx)
industries.note: The bill bans their price-based compensation — fees tied to drug prices, retained rebates, and spread between what plans pay and what pharmacies receive — and requires them to pass manufacturer rebates through to plan sponsors. Their core profit mechanism depends on charging plans more than they pay pharmacies and keeping a share of rebates, which is exactly what the bill prohibits.

Any-willing-pharmacy rules and enforceable contract standards give them guaranteed network access and a complaint process against low reimbursement and unfair terms, which matters as independent pharmacies close and communities lose drugstores.

industries.industry: Health insurers and Medicare Part D plan sponsors
industries.note: They gain tools to audit and penalize their PBMs and to recover disgorged money, but they also bear new compliance, certification, and reporting duties, and many large insurers own the very PBMs being regulated.

The bill requires semiannual plain-language reports on PBM compensation, rebates, and steering to PBM-owned pharmacies, and lets plan participants request claim-level information — giving employers real data for negotiating drug benefits.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the bipartisan breadth that usually predicts committee interest, but months of silence across three committees is the pattern of a bill without leadership backing. PBM reform remains an active topic in this Congress, so the realistic path is either attachment of PBM provisions to a larger health or spending package or quiet expiration at the end of the Congress in January 2027; standalone floor action is unlikely without a committee vote first.
